newsitem.title: FRANCE: Drought to hit durum yields in southern France.
newsitem.headline: Drought to hit durum yields in southern France.

text.p: A three-month dry spell has irreversibly damaged durum wheat in the key production areas of southern France, with regional crop analysts predicting possible yield losses of up to 40 percent.
In the Languedoc-Roussillon area an ONIC official said average yields for the region might fall by 10 to 20 percent from the 3.6 tonnes per hectare reached in 1996.
"We are becoming more and more pessimistic and the situation could get worse if it does not rain by end-May," he said.
Warm weather has also accelerated crop development, making moisture even more crucial at this stage.
"The harvest may start by June 15, some 15 days ahead of schedule," the official said.
ITCF crop analyst Philippe Braun said the situation in the Languedoc-Roussillon region was "dramatic".

He added, "While average yield for the area stretching from the Herault to the Alpes de Hautes Provences was around 3.2 tonnes per hectare last year, this year it will be below two tonnes per hectare."
Durum wheat sowings in Languedoc-Roussillon are expected to rise to 78-79,000 hectares from 76,600 in 1996.
In the Midi-Pyrennees region analysts predicted average durum yields may fall by at least 30 percent from the 5.2 tonnes reached last year.
"Even if it finally rains, yields will fall by 30 percent," one local ONIC official said, adding the same prediction applied to soft wheat.
"What is clear is that yield potential has been severely hit. It will be a disastrous year," a local ITCF analyst said.
But experts said wide variations were possible in the region depending on soil quality and irrigatation.
Durum wheat area for the region is expected to remain unchanged at 69,000 hectares.
Across France durum wheat area may fall by 2.6 percent to 262,770 hectares in 1997, latest ONIC statistics suggest.
France produced 1.241 million tonnes of durum wheat in 1996/97.
Dry soils have also prevented most farmers from starting maize sowings in the Midi-Pyrenee region. But analysts said there was no reason to worry as the bulk of plantings is usually done in May.

Maize sowings were expected to remain unchanged at 225,000 hectares in the Midi-Pyrennees region, but farmers might decide to sow less maize and more drought-resistant sorghum or sunflower, analysts said.
